source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension (នាយកដ្ឋានផ្សព្វផ្សាយកសិកម្ម), "បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះសណ្តែកបាយ" (Mung Bean Cultivation Techniques handbook), Kingdom of Cambodia, MAFF, published by the Department of Agricultural Extension. Reference list on the closing page cites additional 2003-dated MAFF/agricultural-extension source booklets on mung bean varieties, seed production, and pest management, plus several international references (Plant Resources of South-East Asia Vol. I, 1992; Talekar & Skinner, Field Guide to Insect Pests of Tropical Asia, 1995; Nelson, Insect Pests of Vegetables, Philippines, 1969; Mung Bean Adaptation Trial, Kbalkoh Station 1996-2000, CLV Network; and a 1991 Bangkok workshop proceedings on Yellow Mosaic Virus). No elibrary.maff.gov.kh URL is visible on the scanned pages provided, so none is given here. Uploaded as a 38-page scanned PDF; no embedded text layer, all content read visually from page images. This is Source C for crop/mung_bean in this knowledge base (Sources A-B were processed in Batch 42).
text: Bean pod borer (ដង្កូវស៊ីរួងកូរ, referenced in the source both as Maruca vitrata and as "Crochiphora tesulatis," family Pyralidae, order Lepidoptera) moths lay eggs on flower buds, flowers, or young pods. The egg stage lasts roughly 2-8 days; after hatching, larvae bore into flowers and pods to feed and shelter; the pupal stage lasts about 10 days; total life cycle is estimated at roughly 18-20 days. The source notes this pest is commonly found along riverbank growing areas from December through April in Cambodia. Prevention: cultivate soil around the base to disrupt pest populations; rotate with non-host crops periodically to break the host cycle; use light traps for adult moths; maintain field sanitation; and avoid continuous mono-cropping of mung bean on the same field across successive seasons. Control: active ingredients named include Flubendiamide, Chlorantraniliprole, Fipronil, Indoxacarb, Chlorfluazuron, Chlorpyrifos, and Permethrin.
caveat: The second scientific name given in the source for this pest, transcribed here as "Crochiphora tesulatis," is reported exactly as printed; this does not match a standard accepted scientific name found in common pest references, so it may be a source-side typo, an outdated synonym, or an OCR/scan-legibility issue. Reported as-is rather than corrected, per this knowledge base's standing convention.
